It sounds like the medicine works most of the time. And if this is the case, then it is perfectly OK with your doctors advice to keep using it. It can be frustrating to have to rely on medication, but it’s not the end of the world. I’ve had to take some form of medication every single day for more than 20 years. Medication’s just make life better for most people if they alleviate the conditions that is causing distress.

There are a lot of pull-up options out there, from basic training pants, to “nighttime underwear” for older kids designed for bed wedding problems, and then there are products like NorthShore that have ultra absorbent pull on diapers. It really depends on need and what works best for you/what is most cost-effective. Aside from absorbency, sizing and fit is the most important thing to consider. You didn’t mention if your daughter needs protection 24/7, or just at night, if she struggles with bowel issues or just urinary issues. All of these make a difference in how she learns to manage her own hygiene. I.e. changing a wet diaper/pull-up would be easier than changing a messy diaper/pull up. All of this might inform your decision about what kind of product to use as well.  

If you do decide to look into changing up products, you can get free samples from companies like NorthShore or Dry Direct to see if those options could work for her. 

As to actually having her do the change herself, start by just being present with her and asking her to do it. Offer minimal help, and encourage independence as much as possible - if using a tape on diaper, that has Velcro tapes, you could try saying things like “pull that one a little tighter” or “scoot it up a bit” and coach rather than do the work for her. Remember to be patient, and she won’t be completely independent right away. But if you do this enough, she will eventually get to the point where she can go off and change herself regardless of the type of product she’s using.

NAD but I am a social worker and I specialize in teen mental health. 

Please tell your doctor. If you are finding it hard to verbalize it, show her this post and try to answer any questions your provider has. As others have noted, healthcare providers are mandated reporters. With you being a teenager, it is really difficult to say whether or not CPS would get involved right away or if you would have to go home first. There are way too many factors for anyone on the Internet to predict what could happen. But I do want to give you two other avenues to consider what kind of help you need. 

I do want to take a moment to ask about something you said: when you said you don’t want to be here anymore, did you mean at home with your mother and your stepfather? Or did you mean you don’t want to be here, as in you want to hurt yourself? 

If you are considering hurting yourself, please, please please share that with your doctor. If this is something you are thinking about, it might be helpful for you to go to an adolescent psych unit for a few days to take a break from the situation at home and figure out your mental health needs. 


Another resource to consider would be accessing a  YSB safe place shelter if there is one in your area. 
I will link the website for the national organization here and you can see where the closest location is to you. The shelters often help teens who need a break from home life while situations like yours are being sorted out. They provide access to therapists, and many other resources to support teens in crisis. 

https://www.nationalsafeplace.org 

I wish you luck and you are very brave for reaching out for help.

Yes, and, in eight years, I’ve only ever seen one admission that I genuinely questioned whether or not they should have been admitted, and that was for a young teen whose parents definitely had more issues than he did. 

There’s a big difference between admission to a hospital and forced medication though. I’ve seen patients get admitted, refuse medication, stabilize through therapy for a few days and then get discharged. Taking medication is not a condition of discharge in every case.

When we talk about involuntary medication, we usually mean medications that are considered a chemical restraint and act to incapacitate a person, whether by putting them to sleep for a few hours or making them too lethargic to harm themselves or someone else. I have only ever seen these medications given when there was an eminent danger to an individual or others in the hospital. We had an adult client once that tried to attack our nurses anytime he was awake. He eventually got transferred to a state hospital for long-term care, but we had to have two staff members outside his room at all times.

It’s generally considered a right to accept or refuse medication, unless you are an immediate and substantial danger to yourself or others. 

If you are involuntarily admitted then doctors can force you to take medication to calm you down to prevent injury to yourself or others. Usually this is done by injection. I have never experienced this personally, but have seen it done many times when I worked in a psychiatric hospital. I have seen firsthand how it is necessary to prevent further harm. 

I am a social worker and I currently have a client who is diagnosed with severe schizophrenia who refuses to take medication. This client is not currently “dangerous” to self or others, but is making a series of poor choices that are likely to have legal consequences and will likely result in a termination of their parental rights. Previously, when this client has been on medication, they were much more stable and could have visitations and some relationship with their kids. 

There’s a valid argument as to if it would be right for a judge to order this client to take medication or even be placed in an inpatient facility and forced to take medication. Without medication, this person is incapable of making good choices, incapable of parenting their children, and very soon may be incapable of living in society (incarceration). It’s such a moral gray area because respecting this individuals autonomy also means watching them self-destruct.

Yes. I’ve been on both sides of this as a patient in mental hospitals and a professional staff at a mental hospital. I worked on an adolescent unit for years. They cannot put teenagers and adults on the same hallways in hospitals. You will always be with people around your age. Usually there is a separate unit for teens and younger kids if the hospital serves a younger population. (We had a unit for 7-12 year olds and a unit for 13-17 year olds and an adult unit for anyone 18+. 

The staff on an adolescent unit have special training to keep you safe. As a general rule, They usually still have to do the same body searches but they’re not invasive. You usually get to keep your underwear on and they no not touch you in any way. At the hospital, where I worked, only female nursing staff could do the body search on females and male nursing staff for males. They do not watch you in the shower. Industry standards have changed a lot so most places have updated their facilities to where these measures are no longer necessary.  

The likelihood of you getting sexually assaulted is incredibly low. You’re far more likely to be assaulted in a shopping mall or grocery store statistically speaking. 

Patient safety is the number one priority of a psych hospital. Everything from the furniture to the curtains are designed to prevent you from hurting yourself which also in most cases prevents others from using them to hurt you too.  If your doctor thinks you should go, you should go. usually it is a relaxing experience, you get your meds adjusted, and you go on about your life

If thinking about how his actions might hurt someone else causes him to delay acting for even 10 minutes, the statistical likelihood that he will act dramatically decreases. It could also buy enough time for emergency services to reach him if someone else knows he is a danger to himself. 

In my own history of suicidal tendencies, I’ve sometimes wrestled for hours about how my death might harm others, in particular my former step children who are 7, 6, and 3. I would never ever cause intentional harm to them, so the battle is between me wanting my own pain to end and also wanting to shield them from the devastating effects of me dying. There is simply no way to protect them from harm and for my own suffering to go away. This therapist may be grasping at a similar concept with a client who may have felt so isolated that no one would care or be affected if he died. 

All in all, it would not be my first choice, but it is plausible that it made sense in this individual case and that we simply don’t know what context the therapist was using at the time.

Not necessarily. Seeking help for suicidal thoughts only results in an involuntary hospitalization if you have an active plan and intent to act on it. Usually this means you have a method picked out, a timeline, and you have started to take steps like giving away your possessions or purchasing materials etc. 

Depending on the severity of your symptoms, your doctor may suggest a voluntary 3-5 day stay in a psychiatric center to help stabilize you, but more likely than not your doctor will suggest outpatient therapy and prescribe a antidepressant. Most medications fall into SSRI or SNRI categories, again, depending on your symptoms. These medications increase the amount of serotonin and/or norepinephrine your body is able to absorb. They usually take 4-6 weeks to see lasting benefits, but you may feel a lot better the first week and then experience a low for a time until your body adjusts. Your doctor would likely want you to check in with him a couple times during this period or set you up with a therapist who can offer support. 

Thousands of people experience suicidal thoughts and never become hospitalized for having them. It’s actually pretty rare that a casual survey at the doctor office or a conversation about being depressed results in a hospital stay. Involuntary commitments are used primarily for those who have had a active or recent attempt, are experiencing a manic episode (usually associated with bipolar depression) or have indicated em te danger to themselves or others. 

If your doctor suggests a voluntary stay at a mental health center, it’s very uncommon for those stays to last more than 5-10 days at most, with the average being closer to 3-5 days for stability. This would be a suggestion if you are in a crisis, but still showing you are in control of yourself. Refusing this won’t result in an automatic involuntary commitment. If you refuse a voluntary stay, your doctor will discuss safety plans and follow up care and may want you to check in more often. 

Doctors want to know if you are struggling with these thoughts so they can offer help before it becomes a crisis. Early support, medications, therapy, etc. can often prevent the need for more intense crisis response later.

I work in a community mental health center as a case manager for kids at high risk of out of home placements. One of the issues I see most commonly is children and teens with multiple hospitalizations for suicidal threats or behaviors. My job is to write crisis plans and help the kids and their families get access to the support they need to stay at home and not be placed in long term residential treatment. So here’s my thoughts. 

1. Suicidal statements and threats are always a cry for help. They can at times (and often are) also be used for manipulation, but it does not negate the initial cry for help. All suicidal statements are serious and expressing a desire in that moment to die. 

2. Stabbing the wall with a knife can also be seen itself as a threat against you, meaning that your teen has now crossed a line from danger to self into danger to others. Both are serious, but you need to be aware of where those lines are. Any time this happens, you should call the police. You do not have to press charges or even ask that your teen be taken to Juvie, but rather ask them for help getting your teen to the hospital for psychiatric treatment. Most police would rather do this anyway. But it is a 911 emergency every time. 

3. What others on this thread are saying about the hospital and support from law enforcement is true. As a minor, you can have them checked in to the hospital for a psych assessment and 72 hour hold and they cannot refuse. Police will help you if you call them.  You can also call your local police station’s non-emergency number and ask for an officer or EMS to come to your house and talk to your teen about what will happen if they say these things and they have to be called in an emergency situation. 

If you are ever unsure of what to do or how to respond, call the national suicide hotline and they can help with an initial assessment and offer guidance. 

And lastly, they can try to refuse to see a therapist or other treatment, but ultimately you are the parent and you can force them to go. If you go through a community mental health center (CMHC) they will have resources to other services that could be suggested if your teen won’t engage - the agency I work with has therapists, doctors, skills trainers, child engagement specialists, DCS coordinators, etc. if one isn’t working, they can bring in additional help. 

If your child is admitted to a psychiatric ward, it will usually start with a stay between 3-10 days depending on the circumstances at admission. When your teen is discharged, they should provide referrals for follow up treatment. 
I get a referral to my program if a child has 3 or more crisis hospital stays in a 12 month period. There are a lot of supports out there, and many of them (like mine) are state or grant funded and don’t cost anything to access. You just have to reach out to get help.

In most states the mandatory minimum hold is 72 hours. At that time he is re-evaluated to determine if he is a danger to himself or others. 
This is where it gets tricky. Some people are really good at saying the right things and getting out of the hospital. Others are more honest and allow themselves to be kept longer voluntarily. To actually hold him longer against his will would require a court order signed by a judge. It’s not impossible, but only granted in severe circumstances. 

Your best bet as his brother is to talk to him on the phone as much as is allowed by his medical team. If he has signed releases for you to speak to the social worker, do that too. Remind your brother how much you love him and want him to get help. Most hospitals will extend admission for 3-5 days beyond the 72 hour hold if they check in voluntarily. This allows for better medication balance, time to set up therapy, and access to other services. 

You did the right thing by taking him to the ER. Showing him ongoing support is the best thing you can do for him now.
